items.prompt: How does this unit define "translating capability into vocabulary"?
choices: Restating the same underlying product fact in the specific terms each stakeholder already uses to judge decisions
Rewriting an entire pitch into a different spoken language for an international client on the call
Simplifying technical jargon so a pitch is easier to read, regardless of who ends up listening to it
Adding more features to the product so it ends up appealing to more people at the same time
items.reference:
🗣️ One capability — a single true fact about the product
💰🔧🚀 Three vocabularies — cost, reliability, speed
items.explanation: Translating capability into vocabulary means restating one true fact about the product in the specific terms a given stakeholder already uses to judge whether something is worth doing — not changing spoken language, simplifying jargon in general, or changing the product itself.

items.prompt: In the L1 scenario, what changed between the first meeting (lukewarm response) and the second meeting (a yes)?
choices: The underlying product itself was upgraded with genuinely new features between the two meetings
The quoted price was lowered specifically for the second meeting to sweeten the deal
The same capability was described three different ways, once per stakeholder, instead of one generic way
A different, noticeably more senior salesperson delivered the pitch the second time around
items.reference:
🗣️ One capability — a single true fact about the product
💰🔧🚀 Three vocabularies — cost, reliability, speed
items.explanation: Nothing about the product changed between the two meetings — only the framing did. The second meeting translated the same capability into cost terms for the CFO, reliability terms for the ops lead, and speed terms for the founder, instead of one generic description.

items.prompt: Why is this described as a "within-one-deal" skill rather than a general audience-awareness skill?
choices: Because it applies, per this unit, to literally every conversation a person has, not just sales calls
Because it's about correctly reading who is in the room for one specific sale and reframing one capability for each of them, not about audiences in general
Because it, per this unit, only ever applies to deals involving exactly two people in the room
Because it, per this unit, replaces the need to know your audience at the company level entirely
items.reference:
🗣️ One capability — a single true fact about the product
💰🔧🚀 Three vocabularies — cost, reliability, speed
items.explanation: It's a within-one-deal skill because it's specifically about identifying the individual stakeholders present in one particular sale and reframing the same capability for each of them, not a general claim about knowing audiences in the abstract.

items.prompt: Per the unit, what is a CFO / finance stakeholder typically accountable for, and therefore listens for?
choices: Whether the underlying systems stay running day to day without interruption
The budget, and whether spending is justified — cost, ROI, payback period, budget risk
Whether the company is moving fast enough overall to beat its competitors
How easy the product turns out to be to integrate with existing internal tools
items.reference: 💰 CFO — accountable for the budget; listens for cost, ROI, payback, budget risk
items.explanation: A CFO / finance stakeholder is accountable for the budget and whether spending is justified, so they listen for cost, ROI, payback period, and budget risk — not reliability or speed, which are other stakeholders' concerns.

items.prompt: Which sentence is translated into a CFO's vocabulary, per this unit's stakeholder map?
choices: 'It plugs into your existing pipeline with one config change and no new on-call load'
'It removes the manual review step that currently slows every release by two full days'
"This pays for itself in under two months, and every month after that is pure savings"
'It reduces the number of failure points sitting in your fulfillment pipeline'
items.reference: 💰 CFO — accountable for the budget; listens for cost, ROI, payback, budget risk
items.explanation: "Pays for itself in under two months" is a payback-period statement — exactly the cost/ROI vocabulary a CFO uses to judge whether a purchase is worth the budget it takes.

items.prompt: Per the unit, what is an ops / technical stakeholder typically accountable for, and therefore listens for?
choices: Whether current spending is justified against this quarter's approved budget
Whether the company overall is competitively positioned to keep growing
Whether things keep running day to day — reliability, uptime, integration effort, upkeep
The company's overall external marketing message and brand positioning
items.reference: 🔧 Ops lead — accountable for uptime; listens for reliability, integration effort, upkeep
items.explanation: An ops / technical stakeholder is accountable for whether things keep running day to day, so they listen for reliability, uptime, integration effort, and maintenance burden — not budget or growth figures.

items.prompt: Which sentence is translated into an ops lead's vocabulary, per this unit's stakeholder map?
choices: 'That's about $288,000 a year going straight to mistakes that never should have shipped'
"It plugs into your existing pipeline as one extra check, with no new on-call load"
'That's two full days back on every single release cycle going forward'
'This helps you out-ship competitors who are still doing this entirely by hand'
items.reference: 🔧 Ops lead — accountable for uptime; listens for reliability, integration effort, upkeep
items.explanation: "No new on-call load" and "plugs in as one extra check" speak directly to integration effort and maintenance burden — the reliability-focused vocabulary an ops lead uses to judge a new tool, not cost or growth.

items.prompt: Why does a large, true dollar-savings figure often fail to persuade an ops lead specifically?
choices: Because ops leads, per this unit, don't care whether the company saves money at all, in any context
Because the figure in question is, per this unit, usually inflated and not to be trusted
Because a dollar figure doesn't tell them whether the tool adds workload, adds risk, or adds a new thing to be paged about — what they're actually accountable for
Because ops leads are, per this unit, not allowed to discuss budget topics in meetings at all
items.reference: 🔧 Ops lead — accountable for uptime; listens for reliability, integration effort, upkeep
items.explanation: A dollar figure answers a budget question, not a reliability question — it doesn't tell an ops lead whether the tool adds maintenance burden, new failure points, or on-call load, which is what they're actually accountable for evaluating.

items.prompt: Per the unit, what is a founder / exec stakeholder typically accountable for, and therefore listens for?
choices: Whether the underlying systems stay running day to day without major interruption
Whether the company is moving fast enough to win — speed to market, competitive position, growth
The budget, and whether current spending is justified against it
The technical maintainability of the company's internal engineering tools
items.reference: 🚀 Founder — accountable for competitive speed; listens for speed to market, edge, growth
items.explanation: A founder / exec stakeholder is accountable for whether the company is moving fast enough to compete, so they listen for speed to market, competitive position, and growth — not cost or maintenance details on their own.

items.prompt: Which sentence is translated into a founder's vocabulary, per this unit's stakeholder map?
choices: "It removes the manual review step that currently slows every release by two days"
'This pays for itself in under two months, with every month after that pure savings'
'There's nothing new at all for your team to maintain on your own side'
'Your team currently ships roughly 400 flawed orders every single month'
items.reference: 🚀 Founder — accountable for competitive speed; listens for speed to market, edge, growth
items.explanation: "Removes a step that slows every release by two days" speaks directly to speed to market — the vocabulary a founder uses to judge whether something helps the company move fast enough to compete.

items.prompt: According to this unit, what happens when the right capability is pitched to the right person, but in the wrong vocabulary?
choices: The deal, per this unit, almost always still closes, since the underlying capability is what matters most
The pitch can still fail, because the listener has no way to judge whether it answers the question they're accountable for
The listener, per this unit, automatically translates it themselves into terms they already understand
It, per this unit, only ever matters for genuinely technical products, not simpler ones
items.reference: ❌ Wrong vocabulary — right capability, right person, still no way to judge it
items.explanation: Using the wrong vocabulary with the right person can kill a deal even when the capability is exactly what they need — the listener has no way to judge whether it's worth acting on if it isn't framed in terms of what they're accountable for.

items.prompt: In the L1 scenario's first meeting, the pitch was accurate and aimed at all three stakeholders equally. What was the actual problem with it?
choices: It contained, per the scenario, real factual errors about what the product actually did
It was, per the scenario, simply too long and covered far too many unnecessary details
Being aimed at everyone equally meant it was effectively addressed to no one in particular
It was, per the scenario, delivered by someone too junior to be taken seriously
items.reference: ❌ Wrong vocabulary — right capability, right person, still no way to judge it
items.explanation: A pitch aimed at everyone in the room equally, with no stakeholder-specific translation, effectively answers no one's specific accountability — which is why it can land as "interesting" without producing a yes from anyone.

items.prompt: Why doesn't a listener typically translate a wrongly-framed pitch into their own terms on their own?
choices: Because listeners are, per this unit, generally just uninterested in the product itself
Because most listeners won't do that translation work unprompted, the same reason feature framing fails a single listener
Because it is, per this unit, against professional norms to reinterpret someone else's pitch
Because, per this unit, only CFOs are actually capable of this kind of translation work
items.reference: ❌ Wrong vocabulary — right capability, right person, still no way to judge it
items.explanation: Most listeners won't unprompted translate a wrongly-framed pitch into terms relevant to their own accountability — the same reason a bare feature statement fails a single listener in general, this unit extends that to needing the right translation aimed at the right person.

items.prompt: Per the stakeholder map in L2, what should determine which vocabulary a translation uses for a given person?
choices: Whichever vocabulary happens to sound the most technically impressive in the room
What that specific person is accountable for in their role, not their seniority or job title alone
The vocabulary the salesperson personally finds easiest for themselves to explain
Whichever vocabulary was used successfully in the previous meeting, regardless of who's listening now
items.reference: 🗺️ Stakeholder map — accountability → vocabulary → translated capability
items.explanation: The map ties vocabulary to what a person is actually accountable for (budget, reliability, or speed) — not to their seniority, job title alone, or what happened to work in an unrelated past meeting.

items.prompt: In the mermaid diagram from L2, what does the single box on the left represent?
choices: The CFO's own specific translation of the capability, already tailored to budget concerns
The capability itself, stated neutrally, before any stakeholder-specific framing is applied
The final agreed-upon price of the deal once negotiations have concluded
The founder's own specific translation of the capability, already tailored to speed
items.reference: 🗺️ Stakeholder map — accountability → vocabulary → translated capability
items.explanation: The single box on the left is the capability itself, stated neutrally — the diagram shows three separate paths branching out of that one box, one per stakeholder's vocabulary, without the capability itself ever changing shape.

items.prompt: According to L2, is each cell in the stakeholder-map table an invented claim tailored to sound good to that stakeholder, or something else?
choices: An invented claim designed purely to sound persuasive, regardless of whether it's fully accurate
A true fact about the product, restated in different vocabulary — nothing in any cell is invented
A price quote that happens to be specific to that particular stakeholder in the room
A guess about what that particular stakeholder probably wants to hear in the moment
items.reference: 🗺️ Stakeholder map — accountability → vocabulary → translated capability
items.explanation: Each translated cell is a true fact about the product restated in the relevant vocabulary — translation reframes, it doesn't invent claims or tailor facts to sound better than they are.

items.prompt: What is the first step in the three-step translation method described in L2?
choices: Ask the listener directly what they want to hear
State the capability plainly, with no framing yet
Pick the stakeholder with the most authority in the room and translate only for them
Compare the product to a competitor's offering
items.reference:
1️⃣ State the capability plainly
2️⃣ Identify their accountability
3️⃣ Restate as an answer to it
items.explanation: The method starts by stating the capability plainly, with no framing yet — a neutral, shared fact that every later translation is built from without changing.

items.prompt: In the three-step translation method, what is step 3?
choices: Restate the same capability as a direct answer to the question that stakeholder's accountability implies
Ask the listener directly to translate the capability into their own preferred terms themselves
Add an entirely new feature that specifically addresses that one stakeholder's stated concern
Lower the quoted price to make the overall pitch more attractive to that stakeholder
items.reference:
1️⃣ State the capability plainly
2️⃣ Identify their accountability
3️⃣ Restate as an answer to it
items.explanation: Step 3 restates the same fact from step 1 as a direct answer to the accountability identified in step 2 — no new claim, no new feature, just a reframing aimed at that specific person's question.

items.prompt: How does this unit's three-step method differ from the general "so what" ladder used for a single listener?
choices: It doesn't differ at all — they are, per this unit, exactly the same method under a different name
The same value-level fact still has to be re-aimed multiple times, once per stakeholder, since value isn't singular in a multi-stakeholder deal
It skips straight from feature to value with no intermediate reasoning steps at all
It only applies, per this unit, when there is exactly one single stakeholder in the room
items.reference:
1️⃣ State the capability plainly
2️⃣ Identify their accountability
3️⃣ Restate as an answer to it
items.explanation: Unlike the single-listener "so what" ladder, this method has to re-aim the same value-level fact multiple times, once per stakeholder — because what counts as value differs by accountability even when both listeners are past the bare-feature stage.

items.prompt: Per L2, which of these is a recommended way to find out who's actually in the room before pitching?
choices: Assume every single stakeholder in the room cares about cost the most, since budget usually wins
Ask directly before the meeting who else will be joining and what each of them owns
Avoid asking any clarifying questions at all beforehand, just to save time before the pitch begins
Wait until after the deal has already closed to find out who was actually sitting in the room
items.reference:
❓ Ask directly before the meeting
🏷️ Read titles, then verify
👂 Watch first questions asked
items.explanation: L2 recommends directly asking, before the meeting, who else will be joining and what they own — a normal scheduling question that most people answer plainly, rather than guessing or assuming.

items.prompt: According to L2, why should a title like "VP of Operations" be treated as a hint rather than a guarantee?
choices: Because titles are, per this unit, always inaccurate and should just be ignored entirely
Because the actual scope of what someone owns can differ from their title, so it's worth a short confirming question
Because VPs, per this unit, never actually attend sales meetings in real practice
Because titles, per this unit, change far too frequently to ever be useful information
items.reference:
❓ Ask directly before the meeting
🏷️ Read titles, then verify
👂 Watch first questions asked
items.explanation: A title is a strong hint but not a guarantee, since the real scope of what someone owns can differ from it — a short confirming question early in the meeting is worth the thirty seconds it costs to avoid a wrong guess.

items.prompt: If the makeup of the room is genuinely unclear beforehand, what does L2 recommend as the best first move once the pitch starts?
choices: Deliver the CFO-style, cost-focused framing by default, since it's the most universally persuasive one
State the capability plainly and neutrally first, then watch which follow-up question comes back and translate from there
Ask the listener to state their job title out loud before saying anything else at all
Deliver all three stakeholder translations back-to-back regardless of who is actually present
items.reference:
❓ Ask directly before the meeting
🏷️ Read titles, then verify
👂 Watch first questions asked
items.explanation: When the room's makeup is genuinely unclear, L2 recommends stating the capability plainly first, then watching which follow-up question comes back and translating live from there, rather than guessing a framing up front.

items.prompt: How does this unit relate to "value framing over feature framing", per its own description?
choices: It replaces that unit entirely, per this description, and makes leading with value unnecessary now
It assumes the reader already knows to lead with value for one listener, then covers what to do when there are multiple listeners who'd each translate the feature differently
It, per this description, only ever applies to products that have no clear features to translate
It contradicts that unit, per this description, by recommending feature framing instead of value
items.reference:
🧱 Builds on value framing, doesn't replace it
👥 Adds: which value, for which listener
items.explanation: This unit builds on value framing over feature framing, assuming the reader already knows to translate a feature into value for one listener, and extends it to what happens when several listeners would each translate that same feature into a different value.

items.prompt: Is "catches order errors before they ship" translated for a CFO and translated for an ops lead both legitimately "value" rather than "feature", per this unit?
choices: No — only the CFO version counts as real value here; the ops version is still just a feature
No — both versions are, per this unit, still just features, since neither one mentions a dollar amount
Yes — both are legitimately value, but the translation a CFO needs isn't the translation an ops lead needs
It depends, per this unit, on whether the capability happens to be described using technical terms
items.reference:
🧱 Builds on value framing, doesn't replace it
👥 Adds: which value, for which listener
items.explanation: Both translations are legitimately value, not bare feature — each connects the capability to an outcome the listener cares about — but the specific value a CFO needs (cost) isn't the specific value an ops lead needs (reliability), even though both have crossed the feature-to-value line.

items.prompt: Per L2, when pitching multiple stakeholders together in the same room, what's recommended instead of picking one framing for everyone?
choices: State the capability once, then sequence a short, separate translation addressed by name to each stakeholder in turn
Pitch only to the most senior person present and let them relay the pitch to everyone else afterward
Blend all three translations into one single long sentence mentioning cost, reliability, and speed at once
Avoid mentioning the capability plainly at all and go straight into the single most persuasive framing
items.reference:
1️⃣ State the capability once, plainly
➡️ Then translate for each person, in turn, by name
items.explanation: L2 recommends stating the capability once, then sequencing separate, clearly-aimed translations addressed by name to each stakeholder — rather than picking one universal framing or blending all three into one unclear statement.

items.prompt: Why does addressing each translation "by name" to a specific stakeholder matter, per L2?
choices: It's, per L2, purely a politeness convention with no real effect on how the overall pitch lands
Each stakeholder hears their own answer clearly, instead of straining to extract it from one generic version meant for everyone
It, per L2, mainly just shortens the overall length of the pitch being delivered
It, per L2, prevents other stakeholders in the room from hearing translations meant for someone else
items.reference:
1️⃣ State the capability once, plainly
➡️ Then translate for each person, in turn, by name
items.explanation: Naming who each translation is for lets each stakeholder hear their own answer clearly, rather than having to extract their answer from one blended or generic statement — the same failure mode from the L1 first meeting.

items.prompt: In the L3 worked example, what makes the CFO pitch land, according to the unit's own analysis?
choices: It uses, per this unit's analysis, noticeably more technical detail than the other two pitches do
Every sentence answers a budget question directly: current cost, tool cost, and when it turns from expense to savings
It is, per this unit's analysis, delivered with more visible enthusiasm than the other pitches
It, per this unit's analysis, avoids mentioning any numbers at all, keeping the pitch simple
items.reference:
💰 CFO pitch — current cost, tool cost, payback period
✅ Why it lands: every sentence answers a budget question
items.explanation: The CFO pitch lands because every sentence answers a budget question directly — the current cost of errors, what the tool costs, and when it turns from expense into savings — which is exactly what a CFO is accountable for evaluating.

items.prompt: In the worked example, roughly how long does the tool take to pay for itself, per the CFO pitch?
choices: Under two months
Fourteen months
It never pays for itself
Two days
items.reference:
💰 CFO pitch — current cost, tool cost, payback period
✅ Why it lands: every sentence answers a budget question
items.explanation: The CFO pitch states the tool pays for itself in under two months, based on the roughly $24,000/month currently lost to shipped errors compared to the tool's price.

items.prompt: Why does the L3 unit say the generic "proactive quality-assurance platform" version fails specifically with the CFO?
choices: Because it is, per this unit's analysis, factually incorrect about what the tool actually does
Because there's no number in it to weigh against a budget line, so the CFO has nothing to actually evaluate
Because it is, per this unit's analysis, too short a pitch to be genuinely persuasive on its own
Because CFOs are, per this unit's analysis, generally uninterested in quality assurance as a topic
items.reference:
💰 CFO pitch — current cost, tool cost, payback period
✅ Why it lands: every sentence answers a budget question
items.explanation: The generic version is true but useless to a CFO because it contains no number to weigh against a budget line — it describes reliability, which isn't what a CFO is accountable for evaluating.

items.prompt: In the L3 worked example, what specific fears does the ops pitch pre-answer?
choices: Whether the company overall will grow fast enough to survive against its competitors
Added maintenance burden, new alert noise, and a new single point of failure
Whether the purchase in question actually fits within this quarter's approved budget
Whether any of the company's competitors are already using a similar tool themselves
items.reference:
🔧 Ops pitch — one config change, no new on-call, false flags don't halt shipping
✅ Why it lands: pre-answers ops's real fears about new tools
items.explanation: The ops pitch pre-answers the exact fears an ops lead brings into a new-tool conversation — added maintenance burden, new alert noise, and a new single point of failure — none of which are about money.

items.prompt: In the worked example, what happens if the tool ever flags an order incorrectly, per the ops pitch?
choices: It stops that one order, not the whole pipeline, so a false flag never takes shipping down
It halts the entire fulfillment pipeline company-wide until a human investigates the flag
It automatically cancels the customer's order the moment a flag gets raised on it
It sends an automated alert straight to the CFO the moment a flag gets raised
items.reference:
🔧 Ops pitch — one config change, no new on-call, false flags don't halt shipping
✅ Why it lands: pre-answers ops's real fears about new tools
items.explanation: The ops pitch specifies that a false flag stops only that one order, not the whole pipeline — directly addressing the ops lead's concern about a new tool becoming a new single point of failure.

items.prompt: Why does the CFO's $288,000/year figure fail to move the ops lead, per the L3 analysis?
choices: Because ops leads, per this analysis, generally don't believe cost figures presented by any vendor
Because it doesn't tell them whether the tool adds work, adds risk, or adds something new to be paged about
Because the figure is, per this analysis, factually wrong once placed in the ops lead's own context
Because ops leads are, per this analysis, not permitted to consider financial information at all
items.reference:
🔧 Ops pitch — one config change, no new on-call, false flags don't halt shipping
✅ Why it lands: pre-answers ops's real fears about new tools
items.explanation: The CFO figure fails to move the ops lead because it doesn't answer what they need to know before recommending anything to their team: whether the tool adds workload, risk, or new on-call burden.

items.prompt: In the L3 worked example, what specific inefficiency does the founder pitch point to?
choices: A manual review step that adds close to two days to every release cycle
The roughly $24,000 a month currently being lost to orders that shipped with errors
A general lack of on-call coverage across the company's fulfillment pipeline
The overall cost of hiring additional quality-assurance staff to cover the gap
items.reference:
🚀 Founder pitch — replaces a manual step, gets 2 days back per release cycle
✅ Why it lands: connects to the lens the founder is watching — speed vs. competitors
items.explanation: The founder pitch points to the manual review step that currently adds close to two days to every release cycle — an inefficiency framed entirely in terms of speed, not cost or reliability.

items.prompt: Why does the L3 unit say the ops-style pitch ("one config change, no new on-call load") is beside the point for the founder?
choices: Because it is, per this unit's analysis, factually inaccurate once it's told to a founder directly
Because "easy to maintain" doesn't answer "does this make us faster," which is the question this stakeholder walked in with
Because founders, per this unit's analysis, never care about maintenance costs in any context at all
Because the founder, per this unit's analysis, already knew this particular fact before the meeting
items.reference:
🚀 Founder pitch — replaces a manual step, gets 2 days back per release cycle
✅ Why it lands: connects to the lens the founder is watching — speed vs. competitors
items.explanation: The ops-style pitch is accurate but beside the point for a founder because "easy to maintain" doesn't answer the question a founder walked in with — whether this helps the company move fast enough to compete.

items.prompt: What lens does the founder pitch connect the capability to, per the L3 analysis?
choices: Budget risk and how long it takes the tool to pay for itself in savings
Speed to market and competitive position relative to other companies
Overall system reliability and how much integration effort the tool requires upfront
Employee satisfaction levels and how the tool affects long-term staff retention
items.reference:
🚀 Founder pitch — replaces a manual step, gets 2 days back per release cycle
✅ Why it lands: connects to the lens the founder is watching — speed vs. competitors
items.explanation: The founder pitch connects the capability to speed to market and competitive position — the lens a founder is using in this conversation, distinct from cost or operational risk which they might care about elsewhere but aren't focused on here.

items.prompt: Per L3's Checkpoint discussion, if a salesperson only has time for one sentence, is the 'more impressive-sounding' number always the safer choice regardless of listener?
choices: Yes, per this unit, a bigger number always persuades more, regardless of who ends up hearing it
No — relevance to that listener's accountability matters more than how impressive the number sounds in isolation
Yes, per this unit, but only specifically true in the case of CFOs and nobody else
No, per this unit, because impressive numbers are always assumed by listeners to be exaggerated
items.reference: ⚖️ Relevance to accountability beats raw impressiveness
items.explanation: A correctly aimed but less "impressive" sentence (like a no-new-on-call-load statement to an ops lead) moves that listener further than a bigger dollar figure would, because it speaks to what they're actually being asked to evaluate.

items.prompt: If the ops-style pitch ("one config change, no new on-call load") were given to the founder instead of the ops lead, what's the correct diagnosis, per L3?
choices: It's false once it's told to a founder instead, so per L3 it would need to be corrected first
It's true but aimed at the wrong accountability — it doesn't answer the founder's speed question
It's, per L3, identical in its effect to the founder-specific pitch given earlier in the call
Founders, per L3, always reject ops-style language on principle, regardless of its accuracy
items.reference: ⚖️ Relevance to accountability beats raw impressiveness
items.explanation: The statement stays true regardless of who hears it — what makes it a mismatch for the founder is that it answers a maintenance question, not the speed-to-market question a founder actually walked into the room with.

items.prompt: Per L3's extension discussion, what should happen if the founder in the room is also genuinely accountable for both speed and reliability at once?
choices: Pick whichever single vocabulary is used most often in the stakeholder map and simply ignore the other
A single translation blending founder and ops vocabulary together can be more accurate than picking just one
Refuse to pitch at all until the company formally assigns the two roles to two separate people
Use only the generic, fully untranslated version of the capability in that situation
items.reference: 🔀 The map describes common patterns, not a rule every stakeholder must fit
items.explanation: When one person genuinely holds two accountabilities at once, a blended translation covering both is more accurate than forcing a choice — the stakeholder map describes common patterns, not a rule that every person maps to exactly one row.

items.prompt: Per L3, what should a salesperson do if the payback period is genuinely long (say, fourteen months) rather than short?
choices: Avoid mentioning the payback period figure at all, just to keep the overall pitch feeling positive
Still give the CFO an honest, accountability-aimed number — a vague pitch that avoids the figure reads as evasive and costs more trust
Switch the CFO pitch over to founder-style speed language instead, since that avoids numbers entirely
Lower the stated price without telling the CFO directly, to shorten the payback period artificially
items.reference: 🔀 The map describes common patterns, not a rule every stakeholder must fit
items.explanation: The translation method doesn't require good news — an honest, accountability-aimed number is still the right move even with a long payback period, since a vaguer pitch that avoids the figure entirely tends to read as evasive and cost more trust than the longer number would have on its own.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure modes, what's the risk of reusing one stakeholder's translation verbatim with a different stakeholder in the same room?
choices: There is, per L3's failure modes, no real risk here, since all stakeholders in one deal ultimately want the same thing
It undoes the whole point of translating in the first place — a strong pitch for one stakeholder isn't automatically strong for another
It, per L3's failure modes, only really matters if the two stakeholders happen to know each other personally
It, per L3's failure modes, guarantees that the deal will fail immediately with no chance of recovery
items.reference: ⚠️ One stakeholder's translation ≠ universal — reusing it undoes the point of translating at all
items.explanation: Repeating one stakeholder's translation verbatim to a different stakeholder undoes the entire point of translating in the first place — a pitch that's strong for a CFO isn't automatically strong for an ops lead or a founder, since it isn't aimed at their accountability.
